title_eng: Wearable Strain Sensor Using Conductive Yarn Sewed on Clothing for Human Respiratory Monitoring
abstract:
12628 IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 20, NO. 21, NOVEMBER 1, 2020
Wearable Strain Sensor Using Conductive
Y arn Sewed on Clothing for Human
Respiratory Monitoring
Junyung Park, Student Member, IEEE , Sangki Park, Seongcheol Ahn, Y ujang Cho,
Jong-Jin Park, and Hangsik Shin , Member, IEEE
Abstract — In this study, we fabricated a wearable strain
sensor to monitor human respiration by lock-stitchingstretch-
able conductive yarn onto a textile substrate. We devel-
oped the strain sensor by using conductive yarn consisting
of silver-plated and unplated nylon yarns twisted around a
lycra ﬁber with a lock wrinkle structure that could stretch
after sewing. The slopes of the strain-stress curves of three
fabricated strain sensors with a 10% strain load increased
to 121 kPa, 189 kPa, and 241.5 kPa, and the relative change
in resistance (/Delta1R/R0) of the strain sensor increased from 67%
to 116% and from 8% to 109% by respectively applying more
tension and fewer locks to the conductive yarn. In addition,
as we strained the strain sensor to more than 4,000 cycles, the
relative change in resistance decreased by only 6% from its initial value. A respiration measurement test was conducted
with the developed sensor to monitor four different respiration patterns: slow (10 bpm), fast (30 bpm), deep, and shallow
respiration, and the results were compared to those of reference respiration monitoring devices. Consequently, the
proposed stretchable conductive yarn-based strain sensor worked as well as commercial respiration sensors, and its
feasibility was demonstrated for use in respiration monitoring for daily living.
Index Terms— Conductive yarn, respiratory monitoring, textile substrate, wearable strain sensor.

by measuring the temperature of the breath exiting the nose
or the mouth during exhalation [5]. The respiratory effort
can be measured by wearing a strain gauge on the chest or
abdomen [6]. In a clinical environment, respiration is usually
measured by thoracic cavity impedance or by measuring the
CO2 (carbon dioxide) concentration in the exhaled air [7], [8].
Of these methods, CO 2 concentration meas urements during
exhalation are used to monitor surgical and critical patients
because it monitors gas exchange in the alveoli in addition to
only the airﬂow. To conduct indirect respiration measurements,
an electrocardiogram or photoplethysmogram can be used
to derive respiration based on the respiratory sinus arrhyth-
mia [9], [10]. In addition, respiration has been proposed to
be measured remotely using an infrared camera [11], but
this has not been widely used clinically. All above device,
except for the infrared camera, have been used in clinical
settings, and their accuracy and utility have been proven.
However, there are limitations to their use in daily life, for
which the need to monitor physiological signals is increasing.
For example, nasal thermistors require sensors to be attached
to the nose and mouth, making them impossible to use in
everyday life. Strain gauges are the least expensive, but they

require the bands to be worn to take measurements, and the
large measurement module would be inconvenient for the
user to wear. Meanwhile, thoracic cavity impedance or CO 2
measurements require special equipment and thus cannot be
used for unobtrusive monitoring in everyday life. To remedy
this limitation, researchers have investigated another technique
to measure breathing by using ﬁbers that can be fabricated as
textiles for garments. Merritt et al. and Min et al . showed that
respiration could be measured using a belt-shaped capacitive
respiration sensor made from conductive textiles [12], [13].
These sensors were usable in daily life because they could
measure respiration with ﬁbers that are comfortable to wear.
However, capacitive sensors fabricated with textiles can be less
useful than yarn-based sensors because they can increase the
area of the sensor and are susceptible to dynamic noise.
A wearable strain sensor can detect human movement and
monitor various types of motion in real time [14], [15].
Recent studies on textile strain sensors have used nylon
66, polyurethane (PU), poly styrene-butadiene-styrene (SBS),
polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) and spandex for the stretch-
able component. Poly 3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene polystyrene
sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS), polyaniline (PANI), and graphite
ﬂakes are used for the sensing component to achieve high
stretchability and sensitivity. Knitting, printing, and dip coat-
ing are applied to fabricate the textiles with the integrated
strain sensor. Although these strain sensors show excellent
characteristics in terms of stretchability and sensitivity, they
can cause skin irritation due to their low air-permeability [16].
Yarn-based strain sensors have an advantage in that they are
comfortable to wear and can detect human motion over a
long measurement period because they have better wearability
and air-permeability than other materials [16]–[18]. This strain
sensor can detect the relative change in resistance according
to human motions to monitor the pulse, joint movements,
walking, and breathing [19], [20]. Huang et al . demonstrated
the possibility of taking respiratory measurements from lung
simulators using piezoresistive carbon-coated ﬁbers [21]. Since
yarn-based sensors have a simple structure, they can be
directly to common clothing. However, to ensure the durability
during stretching and achieve a high sensitivity, additional
considerations must be made for the materials and stitching
methods.
In this study we achieve high sensitivity and durability by
fabricating a removable strain sensor with a lock-stitching
stretchable conductive yarn on a textile substrate. The simple-
to-fabricate wearable strain sensor is ﬁxed to clothing and
can detect the breathing rate, and speed of inspiration and
expiration during daily living.
II. M A TERIALS AND METHODS
A. Conductive Y arn Embroiled T extile-Based
Piezoresistive Sensor

around a lycra ﬁber. This structure allows for the tension

in this study could stretch under a strain of 21%, but the range
of change in resistance was very narrow when only conductive
yarn was used, so it could not be used as a conductive material
for the strain sensor. However, by integrating conductive
yarn into a textile substrate using a lock-stitching method,

into a stretchable textile substrate. In the process of the lock-
stitch, the stretchable conductive yarn (lower thread) wound
around the robbin is interlocked with the polyester yarn (upper
thread) hooked up by the needle to form repetitive locks and
stitches.

BASIC PROPERTIES OF THE STRETCHABLE CONDUCTIVE YARN
When the textile-based strain sensor is stretched by an exter-
nal force, tension is applied to the conductive yarn, thereby
increasing the resistance. When the external force applied to
the textile-based strain sensor is removed, the tension applied
to the conductive yarn is released, and the resistance decreases
to its initial value.
The lock on the textile forms a ﬁxed point to prevent the
conductive yarn from slipping away. The conductive yarn,
which is bent and ﬁxed into the textile, stretches by the
tension that has been applied to it. Thus, when the number
of locks increases, the change in resistance decreases because
the conductive yarn is extended from a longer initial length.
In contrast, when the number of locks decreases, the change in
resistance increases because the conductive yarn is extended
from a shorter initial length. During inhalation, as the chest
circumference increases with the expansion of the thoracic
cavity, the strain sensor stretches by a maximum of 21 mm
from the initial length of 100 mm, and the change in resistance
increases by a maximum of 82 /Omega1. During exhalation, as the
chest circumference decreases with a contraction of the tho-
racic cavity, the strain sensor returns to its initial length, and
the change in resistance decreases. By adjusting the resistance
changes with locks and stitches, the wearable strain sensor
exhibits high sensitivity, even for subtle respiratory changes.
To optimize the performance of the strain sensor within
the low strain range ( <10%) that results from breathing,
we evaluated the performance of six strain sensors by adjusting
the number of locks and the tension of the conductive yarn.

textiles using the lock-stitching method, and the strain sensor
